title: THE SLAVE GIRL WHO KNEW WHERE A GENERAL COULD BE HEALED
paragraphs:
THE SLAVE GIRL WHO KNEW WHERE A GENERAL COULD BE HEALED
Naaman had power, wealth, soldiers, servants, and the ear of a king. But when his body began betraying him, the person who knew the road toward healing was the little captive girl standing inside his own house.
There is something almost unbearable about the opening of Naaman’s story.
A powerful man is dying by degrees.
And somewhere inside his house is a girl whose entire life has already been torn apart.
Second Kings 5 introduces Naaman as a great military commander of Aram. He was respected. Successful. Powerful. A man of consequence.
Then Scripture drops a devastating sentence into the description:
וְהָאִישׁ הָיָה גִּבּוֹר חַיִל מְצֹרָע
Veha’ish hayah gibbor chayil, metzora.
Literally, the thought is:
“The man was a mighty warrior… [and] a leper.”
That final Hebrew word changes the atmosphere.
מְצֹרָע — metzora.
A person afflicted with tzaraʿat, the biblical skin condition described by this terminology.
Naaman could command armies.
He could not command his own flesh.
He could defeat enemies.
He could not defeat what was happening underneath his clothes.
He could stand before kings.
But rank could not heal him.
And maybe that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because some of us know exactly what it means to look powerful while carrying something we cannot conquer.
You can have the title and still be terrified.
You can have money and still lie awake at night.
You can lead people while secretly wondering who could possibly lead you out of your own darkness.
You can smile for photographs while something beneath the photograph is falling apart.
You can know how to solve everyone else’s problems and still have one problem that refuses to bow to you.
Naaman was a mighty man.
But Naaman needed mercy.
And then Scripture turns our attention away from the celebrated commander and toward someone the ancient world would have considered almost insignificant.
Second Kings 5:2 says:
וַאֲרָם יָצְאוּ גְדוּדִים וַיִּשְׁבּוּ מֵאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל נַעֲרָה קְטַנָּה וַתְּהִי לִפְנֵי אֵשֶׁת נַעֲמָן
The crucial words are:
נַעֲרָה קְטַנָּה — naʿarah qetannah.
A young girl.
A little girl.
She had been taken captive from the land of Israel, and now she served Naaman’s wife.
Do not read that too quickly.
She was not introduced as Naaman’s daughter.
She was not visiting Syria voluntarily.
She had been captured.
Scripture does not tell us her name.
It does not tell us the names of her parents.
It does not tell us precisely what she witnessed when the raiding party took her from Israel.
It does not tell us whether her parents were alive.
We should not invent what God chose not to reveal.
But the text tells us enough.
She had lost her freedom.
She was living in a foreign land.
She was serving in the household of one of the military leaders of the nation that had raided her homeland.
And then she learned that Naaman was sick.
Think about what she could have said.
Nothing.
She could have remained silent.
Humanly speaking, who could have blamed a captive child for feeling no obligation to help the household in which she had become a servant?
But something extraordinary came out of this girl's mouth.
She told her mistress:
אַחֲלֵי אֲדֹנִי לִפְנֵי הַנָּבִיא אֲשֶׁר בְּשֹׁמְרוֹן אָז יֶאֱסֹף אֹתוֹ מִצָּרַעְתּוֹ
The sense of her words is:
“If only my master were before the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would be healed of his skin disease.”
She knew where Naaman needed to go.
The general had armies.
The girl had a testimony.
The general had political connections.
The girl knew something about the God of Israel.
The general possessed authority over soldiers.
The captive girl possessed information that all his authority could not purchase.
And perhaps the most astonishing thing is this:
she spoke.
The wounded child pointed a suffering man toward hope.
She did not possess the power to heal Naaman.
Elisha ultimately would not possess healing power independently of God either.
The story is about the God of Israel.
The girl simply knew where to point.
That matters.
Because sometimes we think we cannot be useful to God until our own lives look impressive.
We think we need a platform.
A degree.
A microphone.
A following.
A spotless history.
A perfect family.
A dramatic ministry.

But God placed one unnamed captive girl inside a powerful household, and her few sentences helped set in motion an encounter that would end with a pagan military commander confessing something astonishing:
“Now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel.”
The girl could not heal Naaman.
But she knew where hope was.
And Christian, that may be your calling more often than you realize.
You cannot forgive another person’s sins.
You cannot regenerate a human heart.
You cannot resurrect the spiritually dead.
You cannot save your husband.
You cannot save your wife.
You cannot save your child.
You cannot save the friend whose life is collapsing.
But you can point.
You can speak.
You can say, in effect:
“I know where mercy is.”
And for us, the road does not finally end at Elisha.
It ends at Jesus Christ.
Because Naaman’s story carries a pattern that reaches far beyond Naaman.
A powerful man discovers his helplessness.
He hears good news through someone the world considers small.
He travels expecting healing on terms that make sense to him.
Then his pride collides with the simplicity of God’s command.
When Naaman finally reaches Elisha, he arrives with horses and chariots and stands at the prophet’s door.
You can almost feel the importance of the procession.
This is Naaman.
Commander.
Warrior.
Representative of royal power.
Surely the prophet will come outside.
Surely there will be ceremony.
Surely something spectacular will happen.
But Elisha does not even come out to perform the dramatic healing Naaman expected.
A messenger tells him to wash seven times in the Jordan.
And Naaman becomes angry.
That is one of the deepest moments in the story.
Because sometimes we want God to rescue us while preserving our pride.
Naaman had already imagined how his healing should happen.
He says, in essence, that he expected the prophet to come out, call upon the LORD, wave his hand over the affected place, and heal him.
Naaman did not merely want healing.
Naaman had written the script.
Have you ever done that with God?
“Lord, save my marriage—but do it this way.”
“Lord, restore my child—but according to my timetable.”
“Lord, forgive me—but please do not make me confess.”
“Lord, heal what is broken—but do not touch my pride.”
“Lord, use me—but do not humble me.”
“Lord, change my life—but please leave my idols alone.”
We come to God desperate for transformation while carrying instructions for how He is permitted to transform us.
Naaman nearly walked away from his miracle because the path toward it offended his expectations.
And that should frighten us a little.
Pride does not always look like someone saying, “I do not need God.”
Sometimes pride says:
“I need God, but I want Him on my terms.”
Eventually Naaman’s servants reason with him.
He goes down.
He dips himself in the Jordan seven times according to the word of the man of God.
And Scripture says his flesh was restored.
But notice the language.
His flesh became like the flesh of a little child.
There is a beautiful literary echo here.
A little girl helped point him toward the prophet.
And the mighty warrior eventually came out of the water with flesh compared to that of a little child.
The powerful man had to become helpless enough to receive.
The commander had to go down.
The proud man had to obey.
The diseased man emerged restored.
And then something greater than healthy skin appeared.
Naaman returned and confessed the uniqueness of Israel’s God.
That is why this story is not ultimately a primitive medical tale.
It is a story about grace dismantling human pride.
And centuries later, Jesus Himself spoke about Naaman.
In Luke 4, standing in the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reminded His hearers that there were many people with leprosy in Israel during Elisha’s time, yet Naaman the Syrian was cleansed.
The implication was piercing.
Naaman was an outsider.
A Syrian.
A Gentile.
Yet the mercy of God reached him.
And the people listening to Jesus became furious.
Grace can be scandalous when it reaches someone we have decided should remain outside.
That is part of the scandal of the Gospel.
We like grace when grace comes for us.
We become uncomfortable when grace comes for them.
For the enemy.
For the addict.
For the adulterer.
For the prisoner.
For the hypocrite.
For the person who destroyed years of your life.
For the person everyone has already written off.
For the person whose past makes religious people whisper.
But Jesus Christ did not come to build a museum for people who believe they never became dirty.
He came to save sinners.
The cross destroys our boasting because every person who stands forgiven before God stands there because of grace.
Naaman brought wealth.
God was not for sale.
Naaman brought status.
God was not impressed.
Naaman brought expectations.
God overturned them.
And Naaman went down into the water with something no money could cure and came back knowing that the God of Israel was unlike the gods he had known.
Now look again at the girl.
She disappears from the narrative.
We never hear another word from her.
No celebration is recorded for her.
No medal.
No monument.
Not even her name.
And yet her voice remains alive thousands of years later.
Maybe you needed that.
Because perhaps you have been wondering whether anything you do for Christ matters.
Nobody notices the prayers.
Nobody sees you trying to keep your family together.
Nobody applauds the quiet act of obedience.
Nobody knows how difficult it was for you to forgive.
Nobody knows how many times you almost gave up.
Nobody knows that you opened your Bible with tears on the page.
Nobody knows that you are still fighting temptations you are ashamed to admit exist.
Nobody knows how hard it has been simply to remain faithful.
But heaven does not measure significance the way social media measures significance.
God knew the girl’s name even when Scripture did not preserve it for us.
And God knew exactly where He had placed her.
Your scars do not automatically disqualify your witness.
Sometimes the person speaking about hope is speaking with tears still in their eyes.
Sometimes the person pointing toward freedom still remembers chains.
Sometimes the person saying, “God is faithful,” is not saying it because life has been painless.
They are saying it because pain did not succeed in making God unfaithful.
That little girl had every human reason to become silent.
Yet she spoke about where healing could be found.
And someone’s life changed.
Who is waiting for you to speak?
Not preach at them.
Not condemn them.
Not pretend you have everything together.
Just point.
Tell them what Christ has done.
Tell them there is forgiveness.
Tell them the cross is sufficient.
Tell them the tomb is empty.
Tell them shame does not have to write the final chapter.
Tell them repentance is not God humiliating sinners for sport; it is the gracious summons to turn from death toward the living God.
Tell them Jesus receives sinners who come to Him.
Tell them there is grace for the guilty.
Tell them Christ still saves.
Maybe you are reading this and you are not the little girl.
Maybe you are Naaman.
Successful on the outside.
Sick somewhere nobody can see.
You have spent years managing appearances.
People call you strong because they do not know how tired you are.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say “God is good.”
You know how to smile at church.
But there is something underneath the armor.
Secret sin.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Adultery.
Envy.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Greed.
Unforgiveness.
A double life.
A heart growing cold toward Christ.
You have learned to keep the uniform polished while the wound spreads underneath it.
Then hear the Gospel.
You do not need another costume.
You need Christ.
You do not need to become impressive enough for Jesus.
You need to admit that you cannot save yourself.
The deepest human disease is not on the skin.
It is sin.
And unlike Naaman’s cleansing, the cleansing offered in the Gospel was purchased at an immeasurable price.
Peter writes of Christ:
The innocent One carried the guilt of sinners.
The clean One touched the unclean.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
Jesus did not merely point toward cleansing.
Jesus became the sacrifice through which guilty people could be reconciled to God.
That is the Gospel.
Not “fix yourself and perhaps God will accept you.”
Not “be religious enough.”
Not “hide your scandal carefully enough.”
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Trust Him.
The blood of Jesus is greater than the chapter you are ashamed to tell anyone about.
This is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing repentance.
Grace tells the truth about sin and then points the sinner toward a Savior whose mercy is greater.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace found Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed Paul.
The thief beside Christ was dying under condemnation.
Grace met him before his final breath.
And Naaman—the foreign commander with diseased flesh and wounded pride—discovered that the God of Israel could reach even him.
So perhaps the question is no longer whether your past is ugly.
Perhaps the question is:
What will you do when grace comes knocking on the door of your pride?
Will you walk away because God did not meet you according to your script?
Or will you surrender?
Be honest.
Bring it to Jesus.
Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need to know that restoration is possible.
Do not underestimate what one testimony can do.
Naaman’s journey began because an unnamed girl opened her mouth.
Your testimony might become someone else’s invitation to seek Christ.
It does not make someone more loved by God, and nobody can buy spiritual favor.

It is simply one practical way to help support the continued creation and sharing of Christ-centered resources while receiving deeper biblical nourishment, encouragement, accountability, and discipleship content.
Christ is Lord.
The Gospel belongs to Him.
Our first allegiance is to Jesus.

But if God has given you the desire and ability to help this work reach another wounded person, another struggling marriage, another ashamed believer, another seeker, another Naaman hiding underneath polished armor—then share it freely, support willingly, and pray that God uses what is offered for His glory.
Because somewhere tonight there is another person who looks strong while quietly falling apart.
And somewhere else there may be an ordinary believer convinced their voice is too small to matter.
Naaman’s story brings those two people together.
A mighty man who desperately needed grace.
A little captive girl who knew where to point him.
And a God powerful enough to use the voice the world would have overlooked.
Maybe you are Naaman.
Maybe you are the girl.
Maybe, in different seasons, you have been both.
But either way, the answer is not found in your power.
It is found in the God who gives grace to the humble—and ultimately in Jesus Christ, the Savior to whom every biblical story of desperate human need teaches us to look.
So speak His name.
Tell somebody what He has done.
Bring your hidden wounds into His light.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Stop polishing armor over wounds that need to be exposed before God.
And when grace reaches you, do not keep pointing at yourself.
Point to Jesus.
Because sometimes the smallest voice in the room is carrying the message somebody powerful desperately needs to hear.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but when Jesus takes hold of your story, your scandal does not get the final sentence. Grace does.
